newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals trend lower in sluggish trading.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals trend lower in sluggish trading.

text.p: Minor metals trading was largely subdued during the past week as prices tended to drift lower amid the lack of robust consumer demand, traders said.
The Ferroalloy conference in Florida sponsored by Ryan's Notes helped to dampen market activity as many European traders attended the annual gathering.
"Business has been slack and is set to remain so until the end of October," one London trader said.
Molybdendum continued to soften rapidly, while several traders closely eyed the cobalt market believing prices had the potential to fall near-term.
Molybdendum found downside pressure as consumers backed off after recent price surges in both ferro and oxide material.
Overall the market had been running long and traders suggested the latest move followed closely from recent bouts of long liquidation and profit-taking in the ferro market at around $11/$12 a kg.
One trader said ferro could slip to $10 a kg, adding stocks of the metal have started to increase.
"The market has to see destocking before prices can attempt a recovering," a trader said.
A lack of consumer buying also knocked cobalt, while the long-running battle between bears and bulls seemed likely to flare over the coming weeks following a period of price stability.
"Cobalt is building up for a near-term move which I believe may be downwards," one trader said.
The trader said consumers held the key to the cobalt's next direction, believing they would hold off for lower prices.
"They are likely to just cover for the first quarter of 1997 and then back off in anticipation of lower prices," he added.
Others said demand from the aerospace and battery industries were likely to keep the market buoyant towards the end of 1990s.
Several traders noted the forecasts by broker SBC Warburg that cobalt prices were set to tumble as surplus grows.
In its October International Mining Outlook Warburg said cobalt could move from an average $23 per pound in 1996 to $16 in 1997 and $10 in 1998.
The broker also expected the world market balance to shift to a surplus of 1,286 tonnes this year following a deficit of 670 tonnes in 1995.
Elsewhere, the Cobalt Development institute figures (CDI) showed first half 1996 world output increased to 10,795 tonnes, versus 7,790 tonnes in the same period of 1995.
Antimony stayed under pressure, though trading was quiet.
Traders said they expected the market to fall and test levels below $2,000 near-term.
One trader said there were rumours of an offer for a small parcel of material at $1,950 a tonne, though this remained unconfirmed.

Both vanadium pentoxide and ferro showed signs of slipping amid ample supplies from China and Russia, while tungsten ferro moved towards support at $5.00 a kg in the face of Russian metal availability.
